content: Scars are areas of fibrous tissue that replace normal skin or other tissues after an injury. They form as a result of the biological process of wound repair in the skin and other tissues of the body. Scarring is a natural part of the healing process. Any injury to the skin, whether from an accident, disease, or surgery, will result in some degree of scarring. However, scar tissue is not identical to the original tissue it replaces and is generally of inferior functional quality. For instance, scars on the skin are less resistant to ultraviolet radiation, and sweat glands and hair follicles do not regenerate within scar tissue. In the case of a myocardial infarction (commonly known as a heart attack), scar formation in the heart muscle can lead to a loss of muscular power and potentially heart failure. In contrast, some tissues, such as bone, can heal without structural or functional deterioration and may even become stronger after a fracture. The term scar originates from the Greek word eschara, meaning place of fire or fireplace. How Scarring Occurs Scars are a natural part of the healing process. Skin scars form when the deeper, thicker layer of the skin, known as the dermis, is damaged. The severity of the scar correlates with the extent of the damage. Most skin scars are flat, pale, and leave a visible trace of the original injury. The redness that often follows a skin injury is not a scar and is usually temporary, though it may persist for a few days to several years in rare cases. Various treatments can expedite the resolution of redness in severe cases. Scars form differently depending on the location of the injury and the age of the individual. To repair the damage, the body produces new collagen fibers, a naturally occurring protein. However, the body cannot replicate the original tissue exactly, so the new scar tissue has a different texture and quality than the surrounding normal tissue. A wound does not become a scar until it has completely healed. Transforming Growth Factors (TGFs) play a critical role in scar development, and current research is exploring ways to manipulate these factors to prevent scarring during the wound healing process. Abnormal Scars Two types of scars result from the overproduction of collagen, leading to raised scars. Hypertrophic scars appear as red, raised lumps on the skin but do not extend beyond the boundaries of the original wound. They often improve in appearance over time. Keloid scars, on the other hand, are more severe and can grow indefinitely into large, tumor-like (though benign) growths. Both hypertrophic and keloid scars are more common in younger individuals and those with darker skin. While they can occur in anyone, some individuals have a genetic predisposition to these types of scarring. They can result from surgery, accidents, or acne, and keloid scars may also develop from body piercings. In some cases, keloid scars form spontaneously. Although they can be a cosmetic concern, keloid scars are harmless, painless, and non-contagious. They are most commonly found on the shoulders and chest and are more prevalent among individuals of Asian or African descent. Alternatively, scars can take the form of sunken recesses in the skin, giving a pitted appearance. This type of scarring occurs when underlying structures, such as fat or muscle, are lost. It is commonly associated with acne but can also result from chickenpox, surgery, or accidents. Scars can also appear as stretched skin, often caused by rapid skin stretching (e.g., during pregnancy, significant weight gain, or adolescent growth spurts) or tension on the skin during the healing process, particularly near joints. This type of scar typically improves in appearance over time. Treatments for Skin Scars No scar can be completely removed, but its appearance can be improved through various methods: 1. Surgery: Scars, such as acne scars, can be excised and sutured in a procedure called scar revision. 2. Laser Surgery and Resurfacing: The use of lasers on scars is an experimental treatment. Vascular lasers may reduce the redness of scars, and carbon dioxide lasers may help flatten scars, though this approach remains highly experimental. The Fraxel laser has been FDA-approved for treating acne scars. 3. Steroid Injections: Long-term steroid injections under medical supervision can help flatten and soften keloid or hypertrophic scars. The steroid is injected directly into the scar, with minimal absorption into the bloodstream, resulting in minor side effects. This treatment is repeated at 4-6 week intervals. 4. Pressure Garments: These are primarily used for burn scars covering large areas and are effective only on recent scars. Custom-made from elastic materials, pressure garments fit tightly around the scarring and are most effective when worn 24 hours a day for six to twelve months. They work by applying constant pressure to surface blood vessels, eventually flattening and softening the scars. 5. Radiotherapy: Low-dose, superficial radiotherapy is used to prevent the recurrence of severe keloid and hypertrophic scarring. While effective, it is reserved for extreme cases due to the risk of long-term side effects. 6. Dermabrasion: This involves removing the surface of the skin with specialized equipment, often under general anesthesia. It is useful for raised scars but less effective for sunken scars. 7. Collagen Injections: These can raise sunken scars to the level of surrounding skin. However, the effects are temporary, requiring regular repetition, and there is a risk of allergic reactions in some individuals. 8. Other Treatments: Silicone gel sheets, when worn regularly, can help flatten and soften raised scars. Silicone, pressure, occlusion, topical cortisone, and vitamin E have all been shown to reduce collagen formation in scars. Chemical peels performed by dermatologists using glycolic acid can minimize acne scarring. Intentional Scarring The permanence of scarring has led to its intentional use as a form of body art in some cultures and subcultures, a practice known as scarification. Evidence of ritual scarring practices can be found in many tribes and cultures worldwide.
